Where it began

Richie Benaud was born on 6 October 1930 in Penrith, New South Wales. Cricket ran in the family. His father Lou was a club leg-spinner who once took all twenty wickets in a match, and under his eye young Richie learned the leg break, the googly and the topspinner. His younger brother John went on to play Test cricket for Australia too.

He played first grade for Cumberland at 16, chiefly as a batsman, and first appeared for New South Wales in 1948–49.

The player

His Test career started slowly. On the 1953 tour of England he made 15 runs in the Tests at an average of 3.00, a figure a man learns to smile about later. The turn came in the West Indies in 1954–55, when he hit a hundred at Kingston in 78 minutes. In India in 1956–57 he took 7 for 72 at Madras, his best Test figures, and on the 1957–58 tour of South Africa he took 106 wickets, beating a record held by Sydney Barnes.

In 63 Tests from 1952 to 1964 he scored 2,201 runs at 24.46, with three hundreds, and took 248 wickets at 27.03. In 1963 he became the first man to reach both 2,000 runs and 200 wickets in Tests.

The captain

He took charge in 1958–59 and won the Ashes back 4–0. In 28 Tests as captain he won 12 and lost only four, and Australia never lost a series under him. He played to win. In the 1960–61 series against the West Indies, he and Alan Davidson went for victory at Brisbane instead of a safe draw, and the game finished as Test cricket's first tie. At Old Trafford in 1961, with England chasing well, he went round the wicket into the footmarks and took 6 for 70 to keep the Ashes.

He got the ball to bounce, hid his googly well and was among the first spinners to bowl round the wicket, a habit that later influenced Shane Warne. He also hugged teammates when wickets fell, rare in his day.

Away from the middle

He trained as a BBC presenter after the 1956 tour and was first heard on BBC radio in 1960. He went on to commentate for decades with the BBC, Channel 4 and the Nine Network, and reckoned he had played in or called some 500 Tests. The cream jacket was Kerry Packer's idea. At Lord's in 1999 he left the microphone to Ian Smith so a New Zealander could describe his own country's win.

He was appointed OBE in 1961, was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1962, and entered the Sport Australia Hall of Fame. He died in 2015, aged 84.

And finally

Touring New Zealand in 1957, he went into a pharmacy in Timaru to find something for his spinning fingers, which his action had torn for years. The pharmacist, Ivan James, recommended calamine lotion and boracic acid. The cure was immediate, and Benaud relied on it for the rest of his career. Few chemists have done more for Australian cricket.
